graph-memory.heading: What is the graph remembering?
graph-memory.text: The discussions describe several different jobs for connected memory. A news graph links people, companies and stories over time. A conversation graph retains speaker-attributed opinions. A shared agent graph records discoveries and useful routes through work. They all preserve connections, but the material being remembered and the person using it differ.

graph-memory.heading: Memory for an agent, or understanding for a person?
graph-memory.text: The repository-learning example shifts the purpose again: a graph can help a developer understand concepts and architectural choices in agent-built code. That is a different goal from giving an agent reusable operational context. This guide keeps those applications separate rather than treating every graph as the same memory system.

agent-continuity.heading: What persists when a runtime ends?
agent-continuity.text: One approach uses fresh agents for bounded tasks and carries useful context forward. Another puts personality, authorised access and tools in a persistent record layer, then creates compute for each turn. Both separate continuity of work from keeping one long-running agent session alive.

agent-continuity.heading: A persistent computer is a different tradeoff
agent-continuity.text: The archive also considers giving an assistant its own continuing computer. Pete describes capability and convenience benefits alongside cost and isolation tradeoffs, while disposable workers allow bursts of bounded work. These are competing deployment choices and tentative assessments, not a single agreed architecture or a verified comparison of suppliers.

code-first-workflows.heading: Preserve a route once it is understood
code-first-workflows.text: A recurring proposal is to use agents while discovering how to do something, then encode the repeatable parts in software. The distinction is between open-ended exploration and recurring execution: discovering sources or a remedy can require judgement, while repeating a settled route may not.

code-first-workflows.heading: Where judgement remains in the workflow
code-first-workflows.text: Code-first does not remove models from the process. The pipeline examples place agents at bounded classification, routing or transformation steps and pass structured results back to code. The source discussions argue for clearer control and less repeated inference; they do not establish that every business task already has a deterministic solution.

human-review.heading: Give the reviewer something inspectable
human-review.text: Review depends on more than a polished final answer. The archive describes intermediate spreadsheets, formulas and other work products that expose how an outcome was produced. Other discussions move interface design toward checking results, finding errors and making corrections.

human-review.heading: Match the checkpoint to the work
human-review.text: Several sources favour short, reviewable increments so people can steer decisions discovered during implementation. One discussion also distinguishes unattended multi-hour work from a small visual edit, where immediate delivery and human judgement may be more useful than a long verification loop. The common concern is retaining direction, not applying an identical review ceremony to every task.

shared-work-layers.heading: Shared work does not require a shared runtime
shared-work-layers.text: The workspace discussions bring people, agents, tasks, documents and files into a common collaboration layer while allowing separate agent runtimes. The problem being addressed is continuity and visibility across many sessions, rather than making every worker use the same underlying agent.

shared-work-layers.heading: Different views onto the same records
shared-work-layers.text: A related proposal uses one authenticated record layer for canvases, task views, voice clients and agent runtimes. Identity-separated workspaces and permissions are part of that design. These discussions describe an architectural approach; they are not independent evidence that every interface or external agent already interoperates with it.

attention-bottleneck.heading: What limits how many agents one person can supervise?
attention-bottleneck.text: Jarad describes agents consuming both token budget and management time: he still has to check what each one is doing. Anthony describes the attention cost of bouncing between concurrent jobs until he loses his bearings. These are different pressures. One adds a queue of supervision work; the other makes it harder to stay oriented inside the work already running.

attention-bottleneck.heading: An agent reviewer leaves a trust decision
attention-bottleneck.text: Andy asks how his supervision capacity can expand alongside swarms of workers. Giving another agent the triage job still leaves him deciding whether that review is correct. His concern is about maintaining a dependable feedback loop as execution expands. It does not show that agent review is ineffective; it identifies the question that delegation alone has not answered for him.

attention-bottleneck.heading: Look for the decisions coming back to you
attention-bottleneck.text: Taken together, these examples suggest asking what decisions and checks return to the person when another job starts. Can the person recover its context, assess its evidence and steer its next step? Those are editorial prompts drawn from the discussions, rather than a tested supervision formula. The archive does not establish a fixed number of agents that one person can manage.

bounded-authority.heading: How can an agent's authority be bounded?
bounded-authority.text: The discussions separate three boundaries: what tools an agent can use, how it obtains information, and what its computer can reach. In episode 64, dpc raises sandboxing and controlled communication alongside destructive actions and prompt injection. That discussion identifies an operating concern; it is not an evaluation of a particular sandbox or a guarantee that isolation prevents every failure.

bounded-authority.heading: Separate gathering the material from analysing it
bounded-authority.text: In episode 69, Pete proposes working out the acquisition route before asking an agent to analyse a supplied body of information. His example contrasts a bounded internal analysis task with an open-ended instruction to find out about a competitor. The boundary is in how the work is assigned and supplied, rather than simply giving the agent a benign goal.

bounded-authority.heading: A restricted account and a restricted computer are different
bounded-authority.text: In episode 79, Pete worries that an agent with limited access to workspace records could still reach material available on a shared machine. He describes wanting separate compute for some tasks that should receive only a limited information set. This adds a distinction between permissions inside an application and access through the surrounding environment. It is a proposed boundary for his setup, rather than proof of a secure implementation.

mature-tool-reuse.heading: When should an agent use an existing tool instead of a new app?
mature-tool-reuse.text: Andy describes a case where repeated attempts to build an application gave way to letting an agent use tools already on his computer. That route worked well for his task, although he also calls it token intensive. The useful comparison is between reusing specialist capabilities and recreating them before the workflow is understood. His experience does not establish that graphical automation is always the better route.

mature-tool-reuse.heading: Delegating tool expertise is part of the value
mature-tool-reuse.text: In episode 76, Andy describes agents using local applications such as Descript and Figma at a level he would not have time to learn himself. He also imagines combining several tools. This is a personal account of accessing existing capability, rather than a benchmark against expert users or a claim that every tool can already be combined reliably.

mature-tool-reuse.heading: A working route can become a software interface
mature-tool-reuse.text: Pete offers a different time horizon. Computer use can demonstrate that a task is possible and valuable; once the route is understood, he expects an opportunity to make it cheaper and more direct in software. Andy emphasises what existing tools enabled immediately, while Pete emphasises what might replace repeated visual interaction later. Read alongside Code-first workflows, these discussions distinguish discovery, reuse and recurring execution without declaring one interface best for every stage.
